To skimp means to use less of something than is really needed or appropriate — less money, less material, less effort, less care — usually to save time or money, but in a way that hurts the quality of the result.

The word almost always signals that the reduction was a bad idea, or at least a stingy one. It's not neutral saving — it's saving in a way you shouldn't.

You will almost always see it followed by "on":

skimp on [something]

This is the standard, natural way the word is used. For example:

  • "Don't skimp on the butter."
  • "He skimped on his preparation."
  • "They skimped on safety measures."

1. Using too little of a physical thing

This is about quantity — putting in less material or ingredient than the job actually requires.

  • "The chef skimped on the cheese, so the pizza tasted bland."
  • "The builder skimped on cement to cut costs, and now the wall has cracks."

The idea here is: a proper, full amount was needed, but someone deliberately used less.

2. Spending too little money

This is about being excessively cheap in a situation where being cheap causes problems.

  • "You shouldn't skimp on a good mattress — you sleep on it every night."
  • "The company skimped on employee training to save money, and now errors are everywhere."

Here, the message is: spending more would have been the right call, but someone chose to spend less.

3. Putting in too little effort or care

This is about cutting corners mentally — not doing something as thoroughly or carefully as it deserves.

  • "He skimped on his essay and got a poor grade."
  • "Don't skimp on research before making a big decision."
  • "She skimped on the instructions, and nobody knew how to assemble the furniture."

Skimp is a mild criticism. When you say someone skimped, you're saying they were stingy or careless in a way that was inappropriate for the situation. It's not a harsh insult, but it does carry a negative judgment.

Compare:

  • "She saved money on the wedding." → Neutral, maybe even smart.
  • "She skimped on the wedding." → Suggests she cut too many corners; it came out poorly.

The difference is whether the reduction was reasonable or whether it crossed a line into unacceptable or noticeably bad quality.

• It doesn't mean simply being careful with money in general. A frugal person who manages their budget wisely is not skimping — skimping implies a specific instance where you gave less than was truly needed.
  • It doesn't mean stealing or cheating — it's more about under-giving or under-doing, not taking something dishonestly.

You'll sometimes hear scrimp used in a similar way, often in the phrase "scrimp and save." Both words suggest cutting back too much, but scrimp tends to suggest personal hardship — someone denying themselves comfort to save money. Skimp tends to suggest denying something to a job, a product, or a situation — giving less than the situation deserves.

  • "She scrimped and saved for years to buy a house." → Personal sacrifice.
  • "They skimped on quality when building the house." → The end result suffered.
How to know you've understood it correctly

If you ever want to use skimp, ask yourself: "Is someone using less than they really should — less than the situation truly calls for — and is the result worse for it?" If yes, skimp fits perfectly.

"Don't skimp on sunscreen." "He skimped on sleep before the exam." "The restaurant skimps on portions."

All of these follow the same logic: a proper amount was deserved, but someone gave less — and it shows.
